combo-leased-spaceport.essay:
Here a foreign operator takes a long lease on land in a willing country and launches from it. This combines two zones that exist on land, leased spots and carved-out zones, with access to orbit. It is the strongest actual example of a launch site working as a place with special status. Baikonur, the largest and oldest, shows how far the idea goes.

Baikonur is in Kazakhstan and was built by the Soviet Union, with the test range founded in 1955. When the Soviet Union broke up in 1991 the site ended up in the new country of Kazakhstan, and Russia wanted to keep using it. Russia sought a 99-year lease, and it agreed instead to pay US$115 million a year for 20 years with an option to extend. The lease now runs to 2050, and all Russian crewed spaceflights leave from there. A second example is being built. Türkiye said in late December 2025 that it had started the first phase of a spaceport in Somalia, on land allocated under a bilateral agreement, chosen because a site near the equator gives rockets an extra push from the Earth's spin. Somalia has only signed the Outer Space Treaty without ratifying it, while Türkiye has joined all four main treaties. Italy's old launch platform off Malindi in Kenya is an older case of a foreign space programme working in another state's waters, and Italy has said it will reopen it.

The settled law is that sovereignty does not move with a lease. Kazakhstan remains the state whose territory Baikonur is in. Under the Outer Space Treaty, a country is liable if it launches or procures a launch, or if an object is launched from its "territory or facility" (Article VII). So a site like Baikonur gives at least two launching states for each launch, the operator and the host. The Liability Convention says the state whose territory is used counts as a participant in a joint launch, and launching states are liable jointly and severally, so an injured party can claim the whole sum from any of them (Article V). Armel Kerrest of the University of Western Brittany says states can share the cost by agreement, for example protecting the host when it takes no real part in the launch, but these agreements do not change the victim's rights. The lease operates between the two governments.

The open questions concern a private operator. All these examples involve states. Nobody knows how much a poor or weak host would be willing to hand a private company in a long lease, or whether a court would treat a clause giving a company wide powers over a leased launch site as lawful under the host's constitution. Honduras shows that such grants can be cut back when governments change, since it repealed its special-zone law in 2022 and its Supreme Court struck the laws down in 2024. It is also unanswered whether a host that is not a treaty party takes on duties merely by leasing to a party. Reading the text, it seems that Türkiye would be a launching state under the treaty for launches from Somalia because it launches. Somalia would not have treaty liability unless it joins the Liability Convention, though it could face claims in general international law. How the two states have divided this between them is not known.

Suppose a private company takes this path. It negotiates a 50-year lease with a government, and the agreement grants exclusive access, an internal security force and light taxation. The company is not a state, so it cannot register anything in its own name. Only launching states and qualifying international organisations keep registers under the Registration Convention. The host must therefore register, or the company's home country must. A US citizen or a company organised under US law needs a US licence to launch from anywhere (51 USC 50904). A foreign company controlled by US citizens needs one for a launch inside a foreign country only if an agreement between the two governments gives the United States jurisdiction over it. British founders fall under the UK's Outer Space Act. If the rocket contains American technology, US export rules apply, and MirCorp, which leased the Russian station Mir, ran into delays in obtaining US export approval for a tether in 2000. The site needs frequencies through the host's membership in the International Telecommunication Union. Once anything goes wrong, the host faces the claim, so it will want a veto over launches. A change of government in the host country may reopen the deal.

Local people are part of the picture. Spent rocket stages from Baikonur fall on the ground along the flight path, and residents there salvage them. Scientific papers report harm to the environment and to people's health from the toxic fuel UDMH used in some Russian engines. A long lease gives an operator power over places whose residents did not agree to it, and that gives future governments a domestic reason to reconsider the terms.

The real potential is that this route exists and has run for decades, with the host earning rent and the operator getting access. Founders could use it to control launch access for a settlement. It gives real physical control over a site and strong practical autonomy. It does not give sovereignty, and the Baikonur rent shows what that control costs even for a major state.

combo-small-state-station.essay:
Ships can fly the flag of a small country with light rules, so people ask whether a station can do the same. A group would launch from some site, then have a tiny state enter the station on its register, and live under that state's nearly empty space law. This is a combination of orbit and the flag-of-convenience practice in shipping. Tonga's history with orbital slots makes it the obvious reference.

Start with what Tonga actually did. In 1987 a businessman named Matt Nilson, who had moved to Tonga, persuaded its king that even a tiny country could apply for positions in geostationary orbit, the ring above the equator where a satellite seems to hold one spot. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency that coordinates radio use, accepts applications from member countries only. Tonga eventually held nine slots and leased them out, and a company called Tongasat ran the business. In 2018 Tonga's Lord Chief Justice ruled that the company had unlawfully received over $46 million in public money. So the small state's right to apply was real, and it stayed the state's right, while disputes grew over who got the benefit. Later filings of a similar kind came from Gibraltar, Papua New Guinea and Bermuda. In September 2021 Rwanda filed for two constellations totalling 327,320 satellites, which shows that a small state can still file for very large systems. Filing for frequencies is a separate act from registering an object, and neither of these cases registered a home.

Registration has a condition the shipping system lacks. Under Article II of the Registration Convention, only a launching state can register an object. A launching state is one that launches or procures the launch, or whose territory or facility is used. So a small country cannot accept any object offered to it. To qualify it would have to procure the launch, which it could do on paper by buying the launch itself or on the group's behalf. Tonga's position also shows a further difficulty. According to the UN's table of 1 January 2026, Tonga has joined the Outer Space Treaty and the Rescue Agreement but not the Liability Convention or the Registration Convention. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty speaks of a "State Party" on whose registry an object is carried. Reading the text, it seems that Tonga could fill that role under the treaty it has joined, with a registry it creates under its own law, and that small states that have joined nothing could not, since the article applies to State Parties.

What is open is whether a country that buys a launch only on paper really counts as procuring it. The treaty does not define "procures". It is also unanswered whether the state of registry must have a real connection to the object. Shipping law has a genuine link requirement (UNCLOS Article 91), although the same treaty does not say what happens if the link is missing, and space law has no such phrase at all. Adrian Taghdiri, writing in 2013, predicted that some countries would write loose rules to attract private space firms, and he warned of debris and of danger to passengers. A presentation to the UN's legal subcommittee in 2016 asked how the shipping concept would fit space objects. No court has ruled on any of this. Reading the text, it seems that a small state could lawfully be the state of registry if it has a real part in the launch, and that registration by a state with no part in it would be open to challenge by others.

What the registry changes is limited. The registering state holds jurisdiction and control over the object and everyone aboard. It is the law of that state that applies, so the founders move from one sovereign to another, and they gain only to the degree that the second one leaves them alone. Article VI still requires authorisation and continuing supervision by the appropriate state. If a small state does none of that, it breaches its treaty duty, and the state in which the founders actually live remains free to enforce its own laws against its own citizens. A US citizen who launches still needs a US licence wherever the launch happens (51 USC 50904), and British founders are subject to the Outer Space Act. The launch site's own country remains a launching state and liable whichever register is chosen, and that country will impose its conditions first. So the launch provider's government decides whether the plan goes ahead at all.

The next steps are as follows. The group pays for a launch from a licensed provider, and the provider's state requires details of who will supervise the payload. A small state with no regulator offers little comfort to that licensing office, and it may refuse if the payload's oversight is unclear. Radio frequencies then need the small state's filing at the ITU, which it has the right to make. Banks would look at the small state's record. Insurers would want a clear legal system. If the station later injures someone or is in trouble, that small country has to answer, and a country with a tiny budget has good reason to set limits. Its law may also change with its politics, and the Tongasat litigation shows that local courts do hear such disputes.

The potential is real but limited. A small state's register gives a station a lawful home, with fewer rules and a more friendly regulator than a large power would provide. The strongest version is a contract between the group and a small state that has joined the Outer Space Treaty, since a private group cannot be a party to a treaty. Under that contract the state actually procures the launch, sets up a small agency and gets paid for it. That produces a privately run station under a friendly flag, with no independence. The state can still change the deal, and the station would have to live with that risk.

combo-igo-register.essay:
The Registration Convention lets someone other than a single country keep a register. An international intergovernmental organisation, a body set up by treaty among governments, can take on the rights and duties of a launching state if it conducts space activities, declares that it accepts them, and has a majority of member states that have joined both that Convention and the Outer Space Treaty (Article VII). The Liability Convention has a similar clause (Article XXII). A project could try to use this route. A group of small states would create an organisation by treaty, and that organisation, rather than any one state, would register and supervise a shared station. This combines places run by international agreement with orbit.

The route exists in practice. The UN's table of 2016 shows objects registered by the European Space Agency (65) and EUMETSAT, the European weather satellite organisation (7), and the office notes declarations by others, including Intersputnik in 2018. So an organisation can register without being a state. It is also settled that the Outer Space Treaty applies to activities carried on through such organisations, and that practical questions are to be sorted out by its parties with the organisation (Article XIII). Liability does not vanish. Under Article XXII of the Liability Convention the organisation and its members that are parties are liable jointly and severally, with claims going first to the organisation and to the members if it has not paid within six months.

This is the most formally solid way of avoiding a single state's register, and it has limits that can be read from the text. The condition about a majority of member states means that most of the founders must have joined both treaties. UN figures of January 2026 give 77 members of the Registration Convention. Many small states have joined neither. UN officials have themselves listed organisations that fail this test among the reasons objects go unregistered. Reading the text, it seems that two or three states with the right memberships could form such a body, and that its status would rest on their real commitment. A treaty body made up of one small state and a private company would not qualify, since a company is not a state.

What is open is how slight such a body can be and still count. The Convention says the organisation must "conduct space activities", and it does not say how much. It also does not settle whether an organisation can be a launching state when it only pays for a launch from a member's territory, though the words "launches or procures" read naturally to include that. Nothing rules out a body set up for one project, and nothing has tested one. It is also unknown how a private company could sit inside such an organisation, since membership of a treaty body is for states, and how far the organisation could delegate its supervision to the company that runs the station. No such body is known to have been proposed, and no government is known to have addressed the idea.

Follow it step by step. Say three small countries sign a treaty creating an Orbital Authority, and it declares acceptance to the UN Secretary-General. The treaty can give the Authority legal personality under the law of its members, although other states need not treat it as anything more than their dealings with it require. It must then obtain a launch. The launch provider's state stays a launching state, keeps its own licence conditions, and will want assurance about supervision. Radio remains with the members, since filings with the International Telecommunication Union go through member countries. A US citizen or US company that launches still needs a licence under 51 USC 50904, because the statute looks at citizenship, and a treaty among other states does not change that. Rocket and station parts remain under export controls, and export regulators will examine a new buyer of that kind.

Residents of the station would be governed by whatever the treaty says. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty speaks of a "State Party", and how this applies to an organisation is covered by Article XIII only in general terms. A treaty among states could make rules for criminal law, as the partners on the International Space Station did under their 1998 agreement, in which each partner keeps legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens (Article 5), with special rules on crime (Article 22). A settlers' assembly might be given real powers by that treaty, and those powers would rest on the treaty, which the member states could change.

The route has some potential. It offers a station with several sponsoring governments, so that no single state's politics can end the project, along with a real legal personality and a right to register. It offers something closer to self-government than a private registration under one state. It also needs several governments to bear unlimited liability for damage on Earth, and most small governments would be slow to accept that for a private group's benefit. The strongest version adds a substantial state or a group of them with real space agencies. The nearest cases are the European Space Agency and the International Space Station, both built by states for state purposes.

combo-lease-on-station.essay:
Under this model a private group does not try to escape the state that registered a space station. It leases space or operating rights on the station and runs its own community there by contract. Residents sign a long agreement that sets the rules, the fees and how disputes are settled. This combines the idea of a lease with low Earth orbit. It is the form most likely to be built, because it asks no government to give anything up.

Two sources explain the idea. One is the ORBIS lease, a model contract drawn up by Spencer MacCallum, a scholar of privately run communities, and discussed by Alexander Salter of Texas Tech University in a 2019 article in the Journal of Air Law and Commerce. Salter starts from Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, which bars any country from taking space as territory, and argues that since states cannot extend territory there, rules for conduct must come from elsewhere, with a proprietary community as the best candidate. The other is MirCorp, which in 2000 obtained commercial rights to the Russian station Mir, with the Russian company RSC Energia as a major shareholder. It paid for the last crew to live on Mir, and it signed up a paying passenger before the money ran out and Russia brought the station down in March 2001. No settlement has used an ORBIS lease.

The settled law sits under any such contract. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty gives the state on whose registry an object is carried jurisdiction and control over the object and its personnel. Article VI makes states answer for national activities and requires authorisation and continuing supervision of private ones. A contract binds the people who sign it. It does not release any government from a treaty, and it does not take away any government's power. The International Space Station shows how registry law works in a shared habitat. Under the partners' 1998 agreement, each keeps legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens (Article 5). The European Space Agency describes modules as treated like the partner's territory, so European law applies in the Columbus laboratory. Article 22 has special rules for crime, under which a country may prosecute its own citizens for what they do in any module.

What is open is how much room a state of registry may leave. Salter reads the ban on national territory as opening a space for private rule-making, and others reply that Article VI keeps private settlers under a country's supervision. Nobody has tested how much supervision counts as "continuing". A US licence requires insurance and permits the government to block a launch on safety, national security or foreign policy grounds, but US rules on occupant safety are largely on hold in a learning period set to end on 1 January 2028. It is also unanswered whether residents can validly sign away rights under the home law, or whether a private lease can have its own penalties. Reading the text, it seems that a contract can decide ordinary matters such as rent and house rules, and that serious crime and safety stay with a state. How a court on Earth would treat a contract clause that removes rights its own law protects has not been tested for a station.

Here is how it would go. A company registered in some state signs an agreement with the owner of a station, or builds its own under that state's licence. Vast's Haven-1 and the planned Axiom Station and Starlab are in this family, although none has flown or seeks self-government, and all depend on government customers or licences. The company writes a lease that sets a common code. A resident signs before launch. The resident's home state still reaches them as a citizen, including through tax in countries that tax citizens abroad. A resident who commits a crime on board comes under whichever state's law applies, and the company has no power to sentence anyone. When the resident leaves or falls ill, the return flight lands in some country, under its law. Children and inheritances would be handled by home countries, since the treaty does not mention them.

The practical pressure is on price. Launch alone, at about $3,246 per kilogram on a Falcon 9, comes to about $3.3 million per person each year for about 1,000 kilograms of food. Aurora Station offered 12-day stays at $9.5 million and closed. By 2013 Bigelow Aerospace had put $250 million of its founder's money into inflatable modules, and it laid off its 88 staff in March 2020. A lease does nothing to reduce that cost, and a lessee depends on the station owner for air and power, with limited ability to walk away. Export rules slowed MirCorp's tether, and the same rules would reach parts bought for a leased module.

The potential here is the largest of the orbital routes if the goal is a community with rules of its own and not a state. A friendly state of registry could leave most internal matters to the lease, in the way many countries let private housing associations or company towns run their own rules, and that could produce a real society with its own daily order. The strongest version adds a clause on arbitration with awards enforceable through courts on Earth, and an agreement with the state of registry about what it will and will not supervise. The limits are that the state remains free to change its mind, and that a resident can always appeal to it.

combo-unregistered-orbit.essay:
Many people assume that a satellite left off the official lists is illegal, or that it floats free of all law. Neither is true, and the difference matters for anyone hoping that staying off a register could make a station independent. This entry looks at what happens when an object or station simply is not registered, whether the launch was licensed or not.

Registration means two things. The Registration Convention, a treaty of 1975 with 77 parties, says that when an object is launched into Earth orbit or beyond, the launching state shall enter it in a national registry and give details to the UN Secretary-General as soon as practicable (Articles II and IV). An older UN resolution of 1961 asks all states to supply such details voluntarily, so the UN keeps two lists. A launching state, under the same treaty, is one that launches or procures a launch, or whose territory or facility is used. The duty lies on that state. The Convention says nothing about private owners and provides no penalty.

The UN's own figures show that gaps are ordinary. In 2016 the head of the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs told the treaty committee that 92 percent of functional space objects had been registered across the two lists, and the same 92 percent figure appears in the office's presentation of November 2018, when 7,514 functional objects had been registered. Non-registration rose from 8 percent of functional objects launched in 2010 to 27 percent of those launched in 2014. The office listed the reasons, among them not being a party, launching states failing to agree on which of them should register, private activity without national regulation, and national mechanisms still unfinished. Crewed spacecraft are customarily registered, and all objects with nuclear power sources have been registered. No state lists all its non-functional objects. Later figures would differ, since launch numbers have grown.

So what the law settles is this. An unregistered object does not become ownerless or free. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty ties legal control to the state "on whose registry" an object is carried, so without a registry that article has no state to name. But Article VI still makes states answer for national activities, and Article VII still makes launching states liable, and neither depends on a register. Failing to register is a breach by a launching state that has joined the Convention, with no effect on what the object is. Resolution 62/101 of 2007 even contemplates the case, saying that if there is no state of registry, the appropriate state under Article VI can pass on information when supervision of an object changes.

The genuinely open point is jurisdiction. If a launching state has failed to register an object, the treaty does not plainly say who holds legal power over it and the people aboard. Kamil Muzyka, writing in Advanced Space Law in 2023, notes that Article VIII may be read as covering all objects, even those not registered, and he also describes registration as the administrative act that makes something a space object in law. Those two ideas pull in different directions. Reading the text, it seems that a launching state or a state with an Article VI duty could still assert authority over its own nationals on board, since nationality law works everywhere, and over the object as owner or licensor, but other states could question its exclusive control. No crewed station is known to have been left unregistered, so a station has never tested this.

Suppose a group buys a launch from a licensed provider and asks that its station not be registered. The provider's country remains a launching state, and it has a duty if it has joined the Convention. Its regulators decide whether registering is required. The 2007 resolution asks states to encourage launch providers to tell owners to contact the proper states. Reading the text, a licensing state has little reason to agree to non-registration, because it stays liable anyway. If the group instead launches on its own from some place with no state support, it faces the problems of parts, port, insurance and radio that any such launch meets. In either case a station needs radio, and an orbital filing is made by a member of the International Telecommunication Union. A station with no filing has no recorded protection against interference, and other operators have no recorded obligation to coordinate with it. Nations track objects in orbit, so it cannot hide, and a large crewed station would be conspicuous to anyone with a radar.

People on board keep their nationality, so home-country laws still apply to them. Article V of the treaty and the Rescue Agreement oblige countries to help astronauts in distress, and they speak of returning them to the launching authority, which a group without a state lacks. A station on no register is also more exposed, and that is the real cost of the choice. Article VIII's rule that objects found elsewhere are to be returned to their state of registry protects a registered owner. An unregistered object has no state of registry for that rule to name. The Rescue Agreement still lets a launching authority ask for the return of an object that comes back to Earth and is found, but a group with no state behind it is not a launching authority. A space lawyer, Michael Listner, has floated a rule under which an object with no registration and no apparent function would count as abandoned and free for removal, and that remains only a proposal.

The potential is therefore small. Non-registration gives no independence, and it weakens the protection the object would have had. The strongest version is an object registered late or registered by a state that keeps poor records. The nearest cases are the functional objects in the UN's count of unregistered satellites, and Swarm's SpaceBEEs, whose problem was radio licensing and not registration.

combo-in-situ-habitat.essay:
Imagine machines mining rock on the Moon or an asteroid and building a large habitat from that material, in orbit or on the surface. The structure itself never left Earth. The space treaties were written around things that are launched, so a home made entirely in space raises a real question about whether those rules reach it. This combines resources from bodies in space with a space habitat.

The words at issue are these. The Registration Convention applies "when a space object is launched into earth orbit or beyond", and it defines a launching state by reference to launching. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, gives jurisdiction and control to the state on whose registry "an object launched into outer space" is carried. It goes on to say that ownership of objects launched, "including objects landed or constructed on a celestial body", is unaffected by their presence there. The Liability Convention says a space object includes its component parts and its launch vehicle, and it does not otherwise define the term. So the text speaks of launching throughout, with one clause mentioning construction on a body.

Some things are clear even so. Article II of the treaty still applies, and no country may take a body in space by claim, use, occupation or other means. Article VI applies to activities and not to objects, so whatever people do in space remains a national activity for which a state answers, with authorisation and continuing supervision. That has nothing to do with whether the item was launched. Article I keeps space free for use by all. The machines that did the building were launched, and they stay under a state of registry. The people came from Earth and hold nationalities.

The open part is the status of the thing built. A paper in the Pretoria Student Law Review of 2021 asks directly how far the definition limited to "objects launched into earth's orbit or beyond" can take in objects constructed in space. It says there is currently no system regulating the status of objects built wholly or partly from lunar resources. Kamil Muzyka, writing in Advanced Space Law in 2023, describes "space-made products" as having similar legal recognition to classical space objects, while noting that the proposal for them has not been adopted. In a footnote on structures built by organisms from Earth on other bodies, he says these might be treated as space objects if national law allows their registration, and he treats the act of registering as what creates the status. The words of the treaty can also be read more narrowly, and no general agreement exists. No court or government has addressed a real case. There is also the unsettled question whether taking local material counts as appropriation, on which states divide. The United States and others say that extraction is not claiming, and critics disagree.

Reading the text, it seems that three positions are possible. One is that a home built in space by a registered machine is a component of or product of that machine, and it comes under the same state. Another is that the structure is outside the Registration Convention, so nobody has a treaty duty to register it, though a state might choose to do so. The third is that the absence of a state of registry leaves it with no state holding jurisdiction under Article VIII, which still leaves Article VI in place for the people responsible. In all three, the operators remain under a state. So the strongest legal effect of the gap is on registration and on who holds jurisdiction, and it does not remove state responsibility.

Consider a real sequence. A company launches its builders under a US licence, or under another country's. That country is the launching state of those machines, and it must supervise the mission's activities. Radio links and tracking are filed through a member of the International Telecommunication Union. The machines work for decades and produce a large shell. Crew arrive on licensed vehicles, each with its own state of registry. A dispute or crime aboard then raises a question that has an answer in nationality, since every person there has a home state with some power over them, and a less clear answer as to the structure. Suppose the group tells its home state it is ending its licence and declaring independence. That state remains responsible for the activity under Article VI as long as those people are its nationals, in the usual reading, and it could prosecute any of them who return. Banks, insurers and suppliers on Earth would remain under its reach. The structure does not need supplies of building material, which is its real advantage. It would still rely on Earth for medicine, parts and new people for a long time.

A second problem is physical. Nothing like this exists, and no machine has built a pressure-tight shell from raw rock in space. The two best-known asteroid mining companies, Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries, ran out of money and were sold. The Stanford torus and Kalpana One are design studies, and neither was built.

The potential is that this is one of the few situations where the words of the treaties actually differ from the facts. A habitat from local material may carry a weaker tie to a launching state than anything built on Earth. A state could fill the gap by registering it as a matter of its own law, as Muzyka suggests. The strongest version is a settlement whose people have children, whose structure was built on site, and which has spent decades with light supervision. It would have a stronger argument than an ordinary station for being more than an extension of its founders' state, while Article II would still bar any claim to the body on which it stood.

combo-captured-asteroid-home.essay:
This idea takes a small asteroid, moves it to a useful orbit near Earth or the Moon, and hollows it out as a home with thick walls against radiation. It combines the law on asteroids with the law on stations. It also raises a question that the treaties were never written to answer, which is whether a rock moved by people is still a celestial body or has become an object.

NASA studied the first half. Its Asteroid Redirect Mission, proposed in 2013, would have sent a robot to take a boulder of about 4 metres from a larger near-Earth asteroid and bring it to a stable orbit around the Moon, for later visits by astronauts. An earlier study at the Keck Institute had looked at moving a whole small asteroid. The 2018 budget proposal called for its end, and NASA announced the close-out on 13 June 2017. Nobody has moved an asteroid, and no published plan for living in one is known.

The law gives clear answers up to a point. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, says outer space, "including the moon and other celestial bodies", cannot be appropriated by claim, use, occupation or any other means. An asteroid is a natural body orbiting the Sun, and it counts. Article VI requires authorisation and continuing supervision of private activity, and the US has a statute under which a citizen commercially recovering an "asteroid resource" is entitled to possess, own, transport, use and sell it, while the same 2015 law disclaims sovereignty over any celestial body (51 USC 51303). The US State Department told Gregory Nemitz, who claimed the asteroid Eros in 2000, that private ownership of an asteroid is precluded by Article II. His case was dismissed without a ruling that decided the wider question. Laws in Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates and Japan follow the American approach of ownership in what is extracted.

The genuinely open point is size. The treaties do not define a celestial body and do not say how big a resource can be. A kilogram of water from an asteroid is plainly a resource under the US law. The whole body might be called a resource if it were small enough to carry off, and there is no agreed line. Reading the text, it seems that a boulder of 4 metres carried away would be treated as extracted material, whereas a kilometre-wide asteroid would remain a celestial body, even if it was moved. Between those lies a range where nobody can say. Another open question is what a moved rock becomes. It is not launched, so it does not fit the words of the Registration Convention, though the machinery attached to it does. It could be argued that the moved body is a space object owned by the mover, and it could equally be argued that any such claim is appropriation by use. No court has dealt with either view, and no government is known to have taken a position on this scenario.

There are also safety rules with real force. Moving a body changes its orbit, so the state responsible has a duty of due regard and of consultation before harmful interference (Article IX), and the Liability Convention applies to damage. Reading that Convention, it seems doubtful that an asteroid itself is a space object at all, since it is neither launched nor made. If it were to strike Earth, the victims would still have Article VI and the general law of state responsibility to look to, and any state whose people moved it would be the obvious respondent. Planetary defence was part of NASA's own study, so governments already link moving an asteroid with public safety.

A project would meet the following in order. It would need a launch licence for the capture craft, from the country of the founders. US citizens need one for launches anywhere under 51 USC 50904. Radio and tracking filings go through a member of the International Telecommunication Union. Any plan to alter an asteroid's orbit would be assessed by the licensing state, and it may well refuse, because the risk it would be accepting has no upper limit. Later, the people who move in would come on licensed vehicles under a state's register. Inside the rock, the law on board would be the law of whichever state holds jurisdiction over the modules and of the home countries of the residents. A company's claim to own the rock would be one more contested paper, since a state licensing the project has to take care not to claim territory by proxy. Article XII also opens stations on celestial bodies to visits by other parties' representatives, with notice, on a basis of reciprocity, which may apply to this one.

The practical side is also severe. Asteroids have very weak gravity, and whether a particular rock could hold air is not known. The two mining companies set up in this field, Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries, ran out of money and were sold in 2018 and 2019.

The potential is that this is one of the few settings in which the words "celestial body" could be tested, and a small moved rock might be argued to be property. The strongest version would use a very small body, with the state of registry for the machinery treating the rock as extracted material, and with international consultation in advance. That gives thick walls and a good legal argument about the material. It gives no sovereignty, and the legal argument would still be untested.

combo-below-100-km.essay:
No treaty says where the air ends and space begins. A craft flying between roughly 80 and 100 kilometres up, or skimming the lowest edge of orbit, sits in the band where aviation law and space law are both arguable. Someone might try to use that doubt by flying where neither regulator can clearly claim the craft. This combines near space, the high seas and orbit.

The basic framework is settled, and the height of the boundary is what is missing. The Chicago Convention, the treaty on civil flying, gives each country full authority over the air above its territory, and it states no height limit (Article 1). The Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, makes space free to all and bars national appropriation (Articles I and II), and it does not say where space starts. The UN's space committee has discussed the line since 1967 without agreement, and some countries oppose defining one at all. Australia, Denmark and Kazakhstan use 100 km in their national space laws. The US armed forces call anyone who has flown above 50 miles, about 80 km, an astronaut. The astronomer Jonathan McDowell argued in 2018 for 80 km as better suited to the physics and to orbits actually flown. Legal writers also describe a functional view, under which a craft on its way to orbit counts as a spacecraft wherever it happens to be, and no treaty has adopted it.

What matters more is a point often missed. The line only matters over a country. Over the high seas, the open ocean beyond national zones, there is no national airspace at any height. UNCLOS, the treaty on the law of the sea, gives every country the freedom to fly over the high seas (Article 87). Space is free as well. So a craft over the open ocean at 90 km is outside national territory on any view, and the doubt about the boundary gives it nothing extra. The doubt changes which rulebook applies to the craft itself. If it counts as an aircraft, it needs a nationality through a register (Chicago Articles 17 to 20). If it counts as a launch vehicle, launching-state rules apply.

There is a real open point here, which comes from the Registration Convention. The duty to register applies when an object is launched "into earth orbit or beyond". A craft on an up-and-down path that never orbits seems to fall outside that text, a reading that fits the words but has not been tested. The Liability Convention has no such wording, but it also does not define a space object in terms of height. So a suborbital vehicle may be a space object for liability without being registrable. Reading the text, it seems that such a craft could end up on no space register, and if it also avoids an aircraft register, on no register of any kind. Whether a state can treat it as an aircraft is the next open question, and no court has addressed it.

Licensing does not have this gap. US law counts a suborbital trajectory as a launch, with a defined "suborbital rocket" (51 USC 50902), so a US citizen launching one outside the United States still needs a licence (51 USC 50904). The UK's Outer Space Act applies to its nationals for launching a space object. A state with national law on the subject can usually reach its own citizens without deciding where space begins.

Physics closes off the appealing part. The zone between 80 and 100 km is where air is too thin for a floating craft and too thick for a stable orbit. Large research balloons usually reach about 40 km. A satellite cannot orbit for long through that much air. A craft can pass through this band for minutes, as space tourist rockets do, or for a short period under continuous thrust, and nobody can stay there. So there cannot be a home in the gap, and a founder is always on one side or the other. Aircraft and balloons below about 50 km are in airspace on any proposed line. Satellites are above it. The Chinese balloon that US fighters shot down off South Carolina on 4 February 2023 was at about 20 km, well below all of this, and an analysis from Leiden Law School treated it as an aircraft in national airspace.

Other government controls also work. Fuel and supplies come from a port or airfield. Frequencies are filed through a member of the International Telecommunication Union. Parts count as defence items under export rules. Anything crossing a national border on the way up is in that country's air under Article 1 of the Chicago Convention.

The potential is small and concerns short flights. A company running up-and-down flights over open ocean might choose among regulators, and a state's own citizens remain under its rules. There is some room for a state to develop this area, for example by registering suborbital craft voluntarily. Nothing about the height band offers a place to live. The strongest version is a licensed suborbital operator under a light-touch flag, which is a business, and no one has claimed independence for one.

combo-unrecognised-state-aircraft.essay:
A self-declared state could set up its own aircraft register, paint its own marks on planes and fly them, including over the high seas. This combines the unrecognised state with the open sky. The aim would be to show one of the visible signs of a country, an airline, with a nationality the state itself created. Real experience with disputed territories shows how this works and what it runs into.

Aircraft nationality works through treaty. The Chicago Convention, the treaty on civil flying, says aircraft have the nationality of the state in which they are registered (Article 17), and that registration in a "contracting State" follows that state's law (Article 19). Article 5 gives flight rights to aircraft of contracting states, and Article 6 says scheduled air services need the permission of the state concerned to enter its territory. Article 1 says each state has complete and exclusive sovereignty over the air above its territory. All of this is settled, and all of it assumes a state that other states accept.

The clearest ruling is English. In 2010 the Court of Appeal decided R (Kibris Turk Hava Yollari) v Secretary of State for Transport. KTHY, which the court described as a Turkish airline, had flown between Britain and Turkey since 1999, and in 2006 it asked to fly directly to Ercan airport in Northern Cyprus, which only Turkey recognises. UN Security Council resolutions 541 and 550 had called on states not to recognise the northern state. The Republic of Cyprus, the recognised government, refused consent. The court held that the Republic has exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above the whole island, though it has no control in the north, and that Britain would breach the Convention if it granted the permit. It rejected arguments that the treaty is suspended where a government has lost control. The airline also relied on the Namibia principle from the International Court of Justice, under which non-recognition should not deprive a people of the advantages of international cooperation. The court held that the case fell well outside that principle, which concerns private rights and everyday administration, and that the principle could not override the Chicago Convention. The appeal was dismissed. The ruling binds English courts only. The Republic of Cyprus has declared the north's airports closed, and trade goes through Turkey.

Open points remain. The judgment deals with flights into a recognised state's territory. It does not deal with a flight that stays over the high seas. Reading the text, it seems that an aircraft with a non-recognised register over open ocean breaks no rule about anyone's territory, since no country owns that air. Other countries would treat it as having no nationality under the treaty, because the state that issued the marks is not a contracting state. There is no general rule about what follows from that over the high seas, and no case has decided it. Whether an unrecognised state's register could count for anything in a third country that chooses to deal with it is a matter for that country. Turkey's position toward Northern Cyprus shows that a single sponsor can allow a route, and in that arrangement the sponsor state's law and permits do most of the work.

Suppose a new project does this. It sets up a civil aviation office and registers one aircraft. Pilots' licences come next. A pilot's licence has to be recognised to mean anything abroad, and the office will not be on the list of bodies other regulators trust. Next is the airport. Without a recognised state behind it, the project has no right to land in any treaty country, so it can fly only between its own strip and places that specifically agree. Aircraft leasing companies and insurers look at nationality and safety oversight, and the aircraft's manufacturer controls parts and technical support. Export rules apply to aircraft parts from many countries. Fuel on foreign ramps depends on a bank that can process the payment, and that depends on sanctions and on regulators. Radio use requires a licence through a member of the International Telecommunication Union, and a country outside the UN can join only with two-thirds of the members agreeing. Passengers carry passports, and a passport from a self-declared state has no code in border systems.

The result, in the cases that exist, is that an unrecognised state's flights run through a recognised patron. Northern Cyprus trade goes through Turkey. An unrecognised place with no patron and no land, such as a floating project, would have even less to work with, since it would also lack an airfield on land.

The potential is modest. A register and an airline carry some symbolic weight, and they can serve real people in a place with an actual population. They might feed into an argument about effective government, since international law takes some account of effective control, an argument the airline made and the English court did not accept as suspending the treaty. The strongest version has a patron state, an airline on the patron's register, and internal flights over the land the state actually holds. That is a working airline, and the nationality in law would be the patron's. Recognition has to be won through other channels.

combo-haps-over-high-seas.essay:
High-altitude platforms are uncrewed balloons, airships or solar aircraft that stay about 20 kilometres up for weeks at a time, doing the job of a low satellite. Most plans place them over land, under the country below. A project might instead hold one over the high seas, the open ocean beyond national zones, serving ships, islands or a floating settlement, with no country below to ask. This combines near space with the air above the open ocean.

The settled rules divide cleanly. The Chicago Convention, the treaty on civil flying, gives each country authority over the air above its territory, with no height limit stated (Article 1). Over the high seas, UNCLOS, the treaty on the law of the sea, gives all countries freedom to fly (Article 87), and the Chicago Convention says its own rules apply there (Article 12). An aircraft has the nationality of its register (Article 17). Pilotless aircraft must be flown so as to keep them from endangering civil aircraft in regions open to civil traffic (Article 8). Radio is governed separately. Paragraph 1.66A of the Radio Regulations defines a high-altitude platform station as a station on an object at 20 to 50 kilometres at a specified, nominal, fixed point relative to the Earth. The ITU Constitution treats frequencies as limited natural resources and forbids harmful interference (Articles 44 and 45). Filings go through member countries.

What is open is how the law treats these craft at all. A 2023 dissertation at the University of Pretoria describes a lack of clarity, because they sit between air law run by national aviation authorities and space law. The Chinese balloon that the United States shot down off South Carolina in February 2023, at about 20 km, was treated by the United States as being in its airspace, and an analysis at Leiden Law School agreed that a balloon counts as an aircraft under the Chicago Convention. Reading this, the better view seems to be that these craft are aircraft, though no treaty says so for this height range. A second open point is the coastal state's position over its exclusive economic zone. UNCLOS keeps freedom of overflight there as well (Article 58), so the coastal state gains no control of the air above that zone. Reading the text, it seems that a platform there is free to stay, though radio signals reaching a country's territory raise a separate question. Whether a coastal country must accept signals from such a platform is a matter for the Radio Regulations and that country's licensing law. Nothing has tested a long-term platform over the high seas.

Loon gives the most useful case. Google's balloon project started in 2011. It signed with Telkom Kenya in July 2018 and then waited until March 2020 for government approval, and because balloons drift, it also signed an airspace agreement with Uganda. It closed in 2021 for lack of a viable business. Stratobus, the French airship, has slipped year after year. These projects asked permission because their customers were on land, and customers are also what would bring this idea into contact with states.

Now the steps. The platform takes off from some country or a ship. That country registers it or requires a registration, and aviation regulators certify it. Stratobus's makers said flight tests had to come before certification and flight authorisation, for a craft with nobody aboard. It needs a frequency filing by an ITU member, which then answers for it. Customers on islands or ships pay through banks in ordinary countries. A ship receiving a signal is under its flag state's law, and a coastal receiver is under that country's. Winds can push a platform off its point, so a platform near a coast must be ready to enter national airspace or lose position. Airspace and traffic rules from the state of registry follow it, and an air defence zone may apply near some coasts.

Service to a floating settlement is the appealing combination. A platform and a sea platform would use each other, the sea platform as a landing or service place and the air platform as a communications link. Each would have its own flag state. That does not produce independence, and it adds more contact points with states.

The potential is real for commercial service and limited for territory. A registered uncrewed platform over open ocean, with one state's frequencies and licences, is likely to be lawful and probably workable, though no firm has shown that it pays. Crewed platforms are a different matter. Above the height where people can breathe the outside air, the craft needs a sealed cabin and carried supplies, and no such craft exists. The strongest version is an uncrewed communications platform for a sea settlement. It would serve the settlement well, and it would give it no extra legal standing, because the platform would remain an aircraft under the law of its register.
