combo-settlement-by-outsiders.essay:
Most space law binds a person through that person's country. So a project could recruit its founders from countries that have not joined the Outer Space Treaty, and have not signed the US-led Artemis Accords, then land on the Moon or Mars. The hope is that no supervising state, no treaty and no set of principles would apply. This combines the bodies themselves with the question of who is bound.

The membership facts are clear. As of 1 January 2026 the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, had 118 parties, and a further group of states had signed without ratifying. Countries such as Vanuatu, Palau, Kiribati, Nauru, the Marshall Islands and Liberia are outside it. The Artemis Accords, non-binding principles for civil activity on the Moon and beyond, had 78 signatories as of 28 October 2026. So many people have a home state outside both. Their home states have no treaty duty to supervise them under Article VI of the treaty. Treaties bind parties.

Nobody has tried this, and several parts are open. The first is customary law, the rules that bind countries because they are generally followed and accepted as law. Ram Jakhu and Steven Freeland examined in 2016 whether Articles I, II, VI and VII of the Outer Space Treaty reach states that never joined, in the context of mining. A piece in Völkerrechtsblog calls Article II customary, and it reports a broad academic view that the ban on sovereign claims also catches private bodies acting with state authority. A claim on the Moon by a non-party's government would therefore be widely contested, even though no court has ruled. The second is the position of people with no state behind them on the Moon. Reading the text, it seems that the treaty leaves such people with no state of registry and no supervisor, and it gives them no rights either. Article I gives freedom of use to "all States". Article IX's due regard rule protects States Parties. A private group with no state has no one to claim those rights on its behalf.

The largest problem is getting there. The Moon cannot be reached without a launch from Earth, and a launch brings in the rest of the law. Any launch site belongs to some country, and that country is a launching state under the Outer Space Treaty if it has joined, with a duty to supervise, and it will ask questions. Only a few countries have launch sites and rockets for this range. Every rocket that can reach the Moon has so far belonged to, or been licensed by, a member state of the treaty. Launching from a state outside the treaty has never been done for a lunar mission. The company that sold a ride would be under its own licence, so it would answer under its home law. A founder who has a nationality from an outside state could still buy passage, and the launching state would then register the craft and hold legal control under Article VIII, with the nationality of those aboard changing nothing.

Suppose the group manages all of this through a non-party host. It lands. Its radios need frequencies filed through a member of the International Telecommunication Union, and other operators then have no recorded duty to coordinate with an unfiled station. Its landing site may lie near an operating base, and the Accords' safety zones, or whatever rules the Chinese and Russian partners set at the International Lunar Research Station, may matter in practice even for those who never signed. Reading the text, signatories' zones do not bind outsiders, but those running them are not obliged to help an unannounced neighbour either. The treaties' rescue duties fall on states and flow toward launching authorities, which this group lacks. Supplies come from Earth, so suppliers are under their home export rules, and rocket parts from US makers need a licence. Its members have home countries that can stop their money, and a country outside the treaty can still pass a law against its citizens doing this if pressured.

The second reason for concern is damage. If a project without a state strikes a working spacecraft, the injured state has no treaty partner to claim against, unless the launching state is identifiable. That is why launching states and major powers can be expected to take an interest in any such project. China and the United States both aim for the area around Shackleton crater at the lunar south pole, so an uninvited group in that region would meet governments with strong reasons to act, though no treaty authorises anyone to remove it.

Nationals of signatory countries are also caught in a different way. The Accords are non-binding, and the Outer Space Treaty is what binds the signatories, so being outside the Accords alone changes little. A national of a treaty party who is merely outside the Accords stays under Article VI through the home state.

The potential is low. The real gain would be for a project with an outside state's government behind it, using that state's freedom from treaty duties and a launch it builds itself. The nearest examples are the ILRS partners, all working through states, and countries' own programmes. Outside the treaties a group gains a weak legal argument against supervision and loses the protection of Article VIII for what it builds. The strongest form would be a non-party state that sets up a real space agency, and that state might then choose to join the treaty for the rights it brings, as North Korea has.

combo-host-state-leaves-treaty.essay:
The Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, has an exit. Under Article XVI, any party may give written notice of withdrawal, which takes effect one year after it is received. So a founder might make a deal with a small state that it would leave the treaty, then host a settlement that claims land on the Moon or an asteroid in partnership with it. This combines a friendly host, or a state that could be bought or persuaded, with the bodies in space.

Part of that is simple. Article XVI is in the text, and any party may use it. No party is known to have used it. Saudi Arabia did leave a different treaty, the Moon Agreement, with effect from 5 January 2024, so leaving a space treaty is something a state can do and does. Withdrawal ends the treaty's duties for that state from then on. Under general treaty law, duties already incurred stay in place, and acts done before withdrawal are still judged under the treaty.

The open question is what is left after exit, and on this people disagree. Ram Jakhu and Steven Freeland discussed in 2016 whether Articles I, II, VI and VII apply to states that "are no longer parties", on the basis that some treaty rules have become custom, meaning they bind states regardless of treaty membership. A writer in Völkerrechtsblog calls Article II customary and cites Hobe and others as calling it a peremptory rule, one no state can opt out of. The same writer floats a half-serious experiment in which trends in US policy might one day erode the rule. A state that has consistently objected to a rule while it forms is sometimes treated as exempt, but a state that signed up in the first place would have difficulty showing that. Reading the text and these sources, it seems that a state leaving the treaty would escape its Article VI paperwork more easily than it would escape the ban on claiming territory, and an open claim to the Moon would be contested by most other states. Nobody knows how a court would decide, since no court has heard such a case.

Other treaties remain. Withdrawal from the Outer Space Treaty leaves the state in the Liability Convention and the Registration Convention if it has joined them, each with its own terms. Its membership of the International Telecommunication Union remains, so it can still file frequencies, and that is an advantage of working with a real state. A state with no space law also has few of its own restrictions, since the new law would be whatever it passes.

Follow the deal. A small government is approached, in the way that Tonga once leased out its orbital slots. Its people have to accept the arrangement, and the country's courts, opposition and media may not. In Tonga, a court ruled in 2018 that Tongasat had unlawfully received over $46 million in public funds, so such deals get reviewed. The notice is filed with the depositaries, the United Kingdom, the United States and Russia. All three would receive it directly, and a year must then pass. Aid donors, trade partners and major space powers will ask questions, and any of them could offer a reason to reverse course. If the plan is to claim land, those three governments have a shared reason for objecting.

Once the state is out, it remains a state, so it can recognise a settlement or claim land for itself. No other state has to accept that. Article II still binds all the remaining parties, so reading the text, they could not recognise national territory on a body without breaching their own duties. Rockets are the next problem. Any launch comes from a treaty party or the host itself. A treaty-party launcher's government is a launching state with duties to others, including the ban on appropriation, and it may refuse to carry a mission whose declared purpose would conflict with its duties. A US citizen or US company that launches needs a US licence wherever the launch happens (51 USC 50904), and the US Moon Express letters of 2016 show how American officials link payload approval to treaty duties. Export rules apply to parts. So a host's exit does not reach the licensing laws of anybody else's nationals.

There would be costs inside the country too. A small state's only space asset may be its orbital slots, its registry or its voice in the UN, and leaving a widely held treaty could damage all of them. A US or European partner might also suspend cooperation with that country. Why no party has left is not recorded, and it may simply be that none has needed to.

Some potential exists. It is the only route where a real state, with real recognition, claims for itself something the treaty forbids its members to claim. That is why the recognition chance is a little higher than for other space routes, since at least one UN member would hold the view that the settlement has legal standing. The strongest version has a substantial mid-sized state and not a very small one, with its own launch capability. The result would be a national claim with few supporters, and it would not be a new independent country. Founders would have swapped private status for dependence on that single government.

combo-safety-zone-possession.essay:
Nobody may own the Moon, yet a base with a large safety area around it might keep other people away in practice. A group could try to build this up over decades, with one announced work zone after another, until it held a stretch of ground in all but name. This combines the settlement of a body with a set of principles written for avoiding collisions. It is one of the most discussed grey zones in space law.

The texts first. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, bars appropriation of the Moon and other bodies by claim, use, occupation or any other means. Article I keeps them free for use by all states, with free access to all areas. Article IX tells states to have due regard for the interests of others and to consult before activities that would cause harmful interference. Article XII says stations on the Moon are open to representatives of other parties, with reasonable advance notice and on a reciprocal basis. Those articles bind parties. The Artemis Accords, a set of non-binding principles with 78 signatories as of 28 October 2026, add safety zones in Section 11. A zone is the area where operations or an unusual event could reasonably cause harmful interference. Its size should reflect the operation and be set by commonly accepted scientific and engineering principles. It is to be temporary, ending when the relevant operation ceases, and signatories should notify each other and the UN Secretary-General. They commit to respect reasonable zones and to coordinate before operating inside them. Section 11 also says they will respect free access to all areas under Article I. The Accords describe this as a way of implementing the treaty.

What is open is how far this can go. No zone has been tested, and no court has been asked. The Accords depend on the word "reasonable" and on self-assessment by the operating state. Critics fear that a zone others must keep clear of could work in practice as a claim, since a site such as a sunlit peak near an ice deposit on the lunar south pole may be the only one of its kind. Supporters, including NASA, say that it respects the treaty, since it only requires notice and coordination. Only signatories have made that commitment. China and Russia lead a separate plan, the International Lunar Research Station, and have not signed. Reading the text, it seems that a non-signatory has no duty to respect a zone under the Accords, and that it does owe due regard under Article IX if it is a party to the treaty. Those two standards may not give the same answer on a real site.

International law on territory adds a further open point. A writer in Völkerrechtsblog notes that courts in territorial disputes have looked for what are called effectivités, acts of real administration such as making rules and running local government, and they have sometimes treated these as strong evidence of title when no one else has a claim. Under the treaty, such acts cannot produce title on the Moon. That writer was discussing SpaceX's terms of service for Mars, and his concern is that such acts of control may be used later, if the rule itself weakens. So safety zones matter as much for what they could be used to say later as for what they say today.

Here is how the process could run. A company under a state's licence builds a base near an ice deposit. Its state announces a zone of a few kilometres while vehicles land and dig. The zone is real and reasonable, because rocket landings throw dust at speed. As the operation grows, the zone grows, and because the base is permanent, the operation does not end. Other missions consult, and coordination takes time and data. A rival's request to work inside is delayed for safety reasons. The rule never says "no", and a late arrival moves elsewhere. Over decades, the base's neighbourhood looks much like private land. Residents make rules for the area, a security office directs visitors, and a registry records who has what. That would be a real practice, even if no one calls it property.

The limits are also real. A state makes the announcement, and a private group cannot make one alone. Licensing and supervision continue under Article VI. The state can change its policy, and other states can demand consultations. Article XII gives representatives of other parties a right to visit stations on a reciprocal basis, which is hard to square with a closed area. If an operator physically blocks another party's lawful mission, that party has a claim of breach against the licensing state, and it has no court with automatic jurisdiction. Harm would be handled by diplomacy, or under the Liability Convention's claims process. A small group could also find a bigger neighbour simply ignoring it. Moon Express's 2016 payload approval shows how US officials handled supervision case by case, with letters that do not bind a future agency.

The real potential is considerable compared with most space routes, and it would come under a state. A safety zone is the strongest available legal argument for controlling access to a stretch of the Moon for a long period, and whether it would hold up for that purpose is untested. The strongest version is a state-backed base with continuous activity, an honest engineering case for its zone, public notices and a record of allowing visits. That provides a working settlement with practical control over its neighbourhood. It gives no title and no independence, and critics would say it comes close to the line that Article II draws.

combo-colony-declares-independence.essay:
Most routes to independence in space try to escape states before leaving Earth. This one accepts every licence and register on the way out, then declares independence once the settlers have arrived. It combines settling a distant body with the law on breaking away, and it has some of the historical logic of a colony that outgrows its parent. Since nobody lives off Earth permanently yet, all of it rests on reading rules made for other purposes.

Some things are clear. Issuing a declaration is not itself against international law. The International Court of Justice said so in 2010 about Kosovo, by 10 votes to 4. That opinion was narrow, and it does not mean that a declaration creates a state or that others must accept it. Self-determination, the right of a people to decide its political status, is recognised in the UN Charter and in later UN instruments, and it applies clearly to colonial peoples and those under foreign occupation. The Supreme Court of Canada's 1998 opinion on Quebec held that international law gives no general right to break away from a state that governs all its people without discrimination. The usual tests for statehood come from Article 1 of the Montevideo Convention of 1933, a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to deal with other countries.

Space law adds its own rules. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, says the state of registry keeps jurisdiction and control over registered objects and any personnel in space or on a body. Article VI makes states answer for national activities. It does not end when a group of nationals stops listening. Neither article has any time limit or distance limit. Article II says bodies in space cannot be appropriated by claim of sovereignty, use, occupation or any other means. All this binds states.

The open part is large. The first question is whether a new state can come into being on a body where the treaty bars appropriation. The prohibition speaks of "national appropriation". A writer in Völkerrechtsblog, citing others, holds that it applies to anyone acting under state authority, and that exercising jurisdiction would count as a sovereign claim. Settlers who had broken away from their state would say they no longer act under it. Reading the text, it seems that the new body, not being a party, would not be bound by the treaty except through custom, while all parties would remain barred from treating any part of Mars as national territory, and that includes recognising it as such. Whether recognising a new state on Mars counts as appropriation by the recognising state has never been discussed by any court. A second question is the meaning of "defined territory". A settlement could say its buildings are the territory, since Article VIII protects ownership of objects, but objects are not territory. The third is whether settlers would be "a people" for self-determination. They would be a small voluntary group of various nationalities in the first generation. Children born there, and later generations, would have a far stronger claim on any reading. The Mars Society has run a design contest for a Martian city state of one million people, and how a settlement could move to self-rule under the treaty has not been settled.

Follow the events. A settlement of some thousands, under the register of one state, passes a resolution of independence. That state's first response is legal. It announces that its law still applies under Article VIII, and that it remains responsible under Article VI. It would be under pressure to show it is supervising, because the treaty requires it. It holds powerful tools, since supply ships, launch licences, spare parts, data links and the settlers' bank accounts all depend on Earth. A Mars transit window comes only every 26 months or so, so a cut-off would take effect slowly and be hard to reverse. Settlers' relatives and property stay on Earth, and the home state can act against them where they are in its reach, and against any settler who returns. The settlers' own treaties, passports and currency would have no standing without a recognising state. The rescue treaty speaks of returning astronauts to the launching authority, which then is the state they broke from.

Force is unlikely, and that is what makes this different from other routes. No navy reaches Mars in less than months. The home state might prefer to negotiate, and Canada's opinion about the duty to negotiate, though about a very different case, shows how law might respond to a clear vote. If a settlement can feed itself, the leverage falls year by year. Other states' interests also matter. A rival power could recognise it for its own reasons, as Russia did for Abkhazia and South Ossetia in 2008, which brought few followers and much dependence.

The potential here is the highest of any space route on the question of independence, while still very low in absolute terms, and it can only arrive late. The strongest version has a large, self-sufficient, multi-generation population, a negotiated transition with the state of registry, a new treaty among interested states revising Article VIII for this case, and a government that has been running its own affairs for decades. Nobody can say when this could happen, and it lies well beyond a 25-year horizon. The route also tends to work best when the parent is willing, in which case the outcome looks like ordinary decolonisation.

combo-company-special-district.essay:
The idea is to stop trying to leave a country and to become, in law, a small piece of its local government. In the United States and many other places, a state legislature creates counties, cities and special districts, which are public bodies with narrow jobs such as water or roads. A company that owns nearly all the land in one spot can ask for such a body and then fill it with its own people. This combines a claim inside a state, a carve-out granted by a host, and the capture of a town. What comes out is real public power, including taxes, bonds, building codes and sometimes police, held by a private owner in practice.

The largest example is Walt Disney World. Disney bought land near Orlando through shell companies, and on 12 May 1967 Florida's governor signed the law creating the Reedy Creek Improvement District and two cities. The district ran land use, building codes, utilities, roads and fire protection. Votes went to landowners, one per acre, and Disney owned most of the land, so it effectively chose the board. The Florida Supreme Court held in 1968 that the law did not break the state constitution.

Some of this is settled law. American courts apply a rule that each voter counts equally in electing local government, and the United States Supreme Court made a narrow exception in Ball v. James in 1981. There it upheld voting by landowners, weighted by acres, for an Arizona water district, because the district's purpose was specialised and its burdens fell on landowners. It is equally settled that ownership of a town does not remove the rights of the people in it. In Marsh v. Alabama in 1946 a Jehovah's Witness was arrested for handing out leaflets in Chickasaw, a town owned by a shipbuilding company. The Court ruled for her and said that ownership does not always mean absolute dominion. And it is settled that a legislature can undo what it made. Florida voted in April 2022 to dissolve the district. In February 2023 it kept the district under a new name and gave the governor the power to appoint the five board members. Pullman, Illinois, ended the same way in an earlier age, when the state's highest court in 1898 ordered the company to sell all property not used for industry, and the company did not fully comply until 1907.

What remains open is narrower than the headlines. Nobody has settled how general a body can be and still keep landowner voting. Ball v. James stressed that the Arizona district was narrow, and Reedy Creek did far more than deliver water, but the 1968 Florida ruling and the 1981 federal case do not answer that for a full city with residents. Disney limited its residents to the two small cities partly from fear that a 1968 case, Avery v. Midland County, would force votes for all residents. The second open point was the agreement Disney and the old board signed just before the state took control, which limited the new board's power and used a clause running until 21 years after the death of the last living descendant of King Charles III. A federal judge ruled against Disney in January 2024 on its suit against the governor, Disney settled the state cases in March 2024, and no court finished deciding whether the agreement was valid.

Now follow the idea through. Suppose a company owns a large tract in a state with a friendly legislature. It first needs a bill, and bills draw neighbours. Blockchains, Inc. owned about 67,000 acres in Storey County, Nevada, and in 2021 wanted a new form of government there, called an Innovation Zone, for a planned 36,000 residents. The governor promoted it in his State of the State address, Storey County objected on money and logistics, critics called it a company town, questions arose about water, and the legislature sent it to a study committee. The company had withdrawn by early October 2021, saying it had spent more than $300 million in Nevada. A company that does get its district still has every ordinary tie to the state. Its staff are citizens, its bonds are sold under securities law, and federal law applies throughout. Reading the text of these cases, it seems that the power rests on continued political tolerance, and that the size of the project raises the price of removing it. Critics of the 2022 Florida law pointed to more than $1 billion in district bonds.

Small places show how far control can go through housing alone. Vernon, California, is an industrial city founded in 1905 where the city owned nearly all the homes and tenants were mostly city employees or linked to them. It had 112 people in 2010. In 2006 outsiders moved in to run for council, the city cut their power and tried to evict them, and a judge let them run, and they lost. State lawmakers nearly dissolved Vernon in 2011, and the Assembly voted 58 to 7 to do so, before the Senate rejected the bill after Vernon accepted reforms and agreed to set aside $60 million for nearby cities. Criminal charges had already reached its mayor and its former administrator. Starbase, Texas, is the newest case. Voters there approved a city in May 2025 under ordinary state rules, with a SpaceX vice-president unopposed as mayor. Outside the United States, the Hawksbill Creek Agreement of 1955 let Wallace Groves and the Grand Bahama Port Authority develop and administer Freeport, under terms extended to 2054. In a partial award reported in March 2026, a tribunal rejected both the government's $357 million claim and most of the company's counterclaims, including the claim to exclusive authority over the area, and it confirmed the government's regulatory authority in Freeport.

The strongest version is a large landowner with a single friendly legislature, a narrow stated purpose, broad public services and long-term bonds. That can last for generations, as Reedy Creek lasted 56 years and Freeport has lasted 71. It gives local power and no separation from the country. Taxes to the higher government, criminal law and the constitution all continue, and recognition by a foreign state is not part of what this route can produce.

combo-investment-treaty-shield.essay:
Most special zones rest on a promise from a government, and governments change. An investment treaty is an agreement between two countries in which each promises fair treatment to investors from the other, and it often lets an investor take a dispute directly to arbitration. Arbitration is a private hearing before appointed judges. The best-known forum is the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, or ICSID, a World Bank body. The idea here is to add a treaty on top of a zone, so that a later government that cancels the zone must pay for doing so. This combines a host's carve-out with protection from outside the host's own courts.

Some of this is clear. A treaty award is about money, and it does not restore a zone or give anyone a right to rule. Using the forum also requires consent, which comes from a treaty or a contract, because ICSID membership alone gives no investor a right to sue. Enforcement has real force, since member countries agree to treat an award like a ruling of their own courts. A country that repeals a scheme investors relied on can lose. Romania adopted investment incentives for certain regions in 1999, and investors built a large food business relying on them. Romania repealed them as part of joining the European Union, and in 2013 a tribunal found a breach of the Romania and Sweden treaty and awarded about £70 million plus interest. The European Commission then ruled that paying the award would be illegal state aid. The European General Court annulled that ruling in 2019, and in 2020 the United Kingdom Supreme Court unanimously lifted a stay so that enforcement could proceed in England. In January 2022 the European Court of Justice overturned the 2019 judgment, and on 2 October 2024 the General Court upheld the finding that the award was state aid, and held that sums already paid could be recovered from any of the claimants. That ruling was open to appeal when it was reported.

The live test is Próspera. It is a private zone on the island of Roatán, set up under the Honduran law on Zones for Employment and Economic Development, or ZEDEs. In April 2022 Honduras repealed the law, and on 20 September 2024 its Supreme Court declared the laws unconstitutional from the start. The owners filed Honduras Próspera Inc. and others v. Honduras, ICSID case ARB/23/2, relying on CAFTA-DR, the trade treaty linking the United States with Central America, and on a legal stability agreement with the state. The first demand was $10.775 billion, later reported as reduced to about $1.63 billion. Honduras left ICSID in 2024 and rejoined with effect from 16 August 2026. The tribunal ruled on preliminary objections in February 2025, and no decision on the merits had been reported by October 2026.

The open questions here are the ones that matter. No tribunal has yet ruled in the Próspera case on whether a promise made under a law later held void from the start can found a treaty claim. The Honduran Supreme Court's ruling treats the zones as never lawful, and the investors rely on promises the state made to them. President Castro's government described ending the zones as recovering sovereignty, and critics and supporters disagree over whether a claim of this kind should exist at all. Paul Romer, an economist who first promoted charter cities, has said Próspera is not close to a model he would recommend. A second open case has appeared in Australia. Landbridge, a Chinese company that holds a 99-year lease of the Port of Darwin, filed a claim at ICSID on 24 April 2026, saying Australia's actions were discriminatory, after both main parties promised in 2025 to return the port to Australian ownership. How that ends is not known. Panama's Supreme Court ruled in January 2026 that the contracts for two canal ports held by a CK Hutchison company were unconstitutional, and the company brought an arbitration claim at the International Chamber of Commerce.

Follow the steps. An investor needs the nationality of a country with a treaty, so the founders' passports and the place where the company is registered begin to matter. Next the host must agree to a stability contract or already have a treaty in force. When a later government moves against the zone, the investor files, and hearings run for years while legal costs mount. During that time local courts and police keep their powers, because a tribunal cannot order officers off the land. Reading the awards, it seems that the treaty shifts the cost of cancelling onto the state and leaves the decision with the state. Banks and insurers can take comfort from a treaty only as far as they believe an award can be collected, and Micula shows collection can take more than a decade after a 2005 filing.

The Sulu heirs' case shows a nearby failure. Eight claimants won a $14.92 billion award against Malaysia on an 1878 contract, and French courts undid it because the arbitrator lacked power. That case turned on whether Malaysia had ever agreed to the arbitrator, so the terms of consent decide whether any of this protection exists.

The route does have potential as a financial deterrent against a poor host, and that deterrent may buy time and a negotiated outcome. The strongest version is a clear treaty between two states, a specific stability contract signed by the proper authority, and a project built so that local people want it to continue. Even that version produces money or a settlement, and the land remains the host's. It has never produced recognition of anything as a state.

combo-associated-state-deal.essay:
Free association is an arrangement in which a small place runs itself while a larger state handles some of the jobs of a country, usually defence and part of its foreign relations. A new founder could imagine using it as a halfway house. A territory would get self-government from a host, the host would keep the expensive duties, and outside governments might gradually deal with the place as a state. This combines a carve-out, the end of colonial rule, and an international agreement.

The working models are clear. The Cook Islands have been self-governing in free association with New Zealand since 4 August 1965, and Niue since 19 October 1974. New Zealand cannot make laws for them, and it acts on defence and foreign affairs only when they ask. They have their own immigration rules, and their people hold New Zealand citizenship. Each signs United Nations treaties and joins UN bodies as a state, the Cook Islands since 1992 and Niue since 1994. Neither is a UN member. The Compact states with the United States went further. The Marshall Islands and Micronesia, associated in 1986, and Palau, associated in 1994, are independent states, and the United States provides money and defence and holds control over who may bring forces in. All three are UN members.

What is open is the legal character of the relationship, and it is argued now. Free association by itself does not decide whether a place is a state. In 2025 the Cook Islands' prime minister, Mark Brown, said the UN had confirmed that his country did not meet membership requirements, and its foreign minister said joining would need a referendum and a new look at the tie to New Zealand. A New Zealand foreign ministry spokesperson said that the Cook Islands is not a fully independent and sovereign state, and New Zealand has said UN membership could cost its people automatic access to New Zealand citizenship. Each document is specific to its parties, so there is no general rule for how a place leaves. The Caribbean associated states of the 1960s asked for and received independence, and Anguilla broke away from one of them and went back to Britain as a dependent territory.

Now consider a founder trying this today. A private group has no territory with a claim to self-government, so it would first need a host's carve-out, and then a constitutional change by the host. Every existing association grew out of a place already under a colonial or trust arrangement, and reading the record it seems the path has been open to peoples and territories, with no example of a private settlement using it. That is an inference from the list of cases and not a rule stated in a treaty. The attempts inside modern states have mostly failed. Spain's Congress of Deputies refused in 2005 to debate a Basque proposal first presented in 2003, and the Philippine Supreme Court struck down a Bangsamoro proposal in 2008. A 1994 treaty described Tatarstan as associated with Russia, and some commentators saw changes to Tatarstan's constitution in 2002 as making it essentially an integral part of Russia. Voters in the Cocos (Keeling) Islands in 1984 had the option and 21 of 261 chose it. Tokelau's referendums of 2006 and 2007 failed to reach the two-thirds needed.

Follow what it would mean in practice. The larger partner's passports would likely be the first thing residents want, and the Cook Islands' experience shows how tightly that ties them to the partner's decisions. The larger state also stays answerable abroad, so it would keep some control over who enters and which treaties the place signs. The Compacts show the price, since the United States holds authority over defence and in return pays large sums. The 2003 renewal gave Micronesia and the Marshall Islands $3.5 billion, and the renewal that became law in March 2024 totals $7.1 billion over 20 years, with Palau included. A new place would have to offer something worth that, such as a strategic location, and few private projects can. Banks and telecoms would likely deal with it through the partner's systems, which reading the arrangements seems the natural result, though a new case would set its own terms.

The potential is small and specific. The strongest version is an existing autonomous territory with a real population that negotiates association after a referendum, with a private developer as a junior partner. Reaching treaty capacity through a long tie, as the Cook Islands did from 1965 to 1992, is the part of this path that actually has a record. It is a route for peoples who are already there, and it takes decades.

combo-treaty-cession-new-body.essay:
The cleanest legal route to a new territory would be this. An existing state signs a treaty handing a piece of its land to a new body, gives up all claim to it, and the new body becomes its government. Title would then come from the one party entitled to give it. This combines buying from a state, an agreement between governments, and the attempt to become a state.

Some of this is clear. States can transfer territory to each other. Egypt announced in 2016 that it would hand Tiran and Sanafir to Saudi Arabia and ratified the treaty in 2017, although the handover has stalled and sources differ on where it stands. Sovereignty over Vatican City was recognised to the Holy See by Italy in the Lateran Treaty of 1929, creating a state of 44 hectares. It is also clear that treaties are made between entities with capacity. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, in Article 6, says every state has the capacity to make them. It says nothing that helps a company or club. And it is clear that a transfer from one state does not bind other states to recognise the result. South Africa declared four homelands independent from 1976, starting with Transkei, and apart from South Africa and the four themselves, which recognised one another, no government accepted them.

The hard part is the recipient. The Holy See was an old international body with diplomatic ties before 1929, and its case is not a pattern for a new group. The closest modern parallel is the 1998 treaty by which Malta gave the Order of Malta, another old body with diplomatic ties, use of part of Fort St Angelo for 99 years. It gave the Order use with listed privileges and it did not give sovereignty. What is open, and has not been tested, is whether a brand-new private body could receive sovereignty directly by treaty. Nothing in the Vienna Convention says that it could never hold title, since a place may become a state by meeting the usual tests of territory, population and government. Reading the text, it seems that a treaty signed with a body that is not yet a state would at first count as a domestic act of the giving state or as a private contract, and that the new place's status would depend on other governments' responses. That reasoning is a reading and no court has ruled on it.

Politics makes the transfer far harder than the law. In the Tiran and Sanafir case, a transfer between two friendly states set off the largest protests against the government since 2014, with hundreds arrested. The Chagos treaty shows how slow it can be, even when a court has spoken. In 2019 the International Court of Justice advised that Britain should end its rule of the islands. On 22 May 2025 Britain and Mauritius signed a treaty transferring sovereignty and letting Britain exercise rights on Diego Garcia for an initial 99 years, for annual payments. Then a change in the American position stalled it, the British bill lapsed in April 2026, and as of October 2026 it was not in force. The same opinion shows a further limit. The court held that Mauritius's agreement to give up the islands in 1965 could not be treated as an international agreement, because it came while Britain ruled Mauritius, and that land cannot be split off without the free and genuine will of the people concerned. Reading that reasoning, a founder would have to expect the people on any ceded land to have a say, and a deal that ignored them would be open to attack.

Follow the steps. A government must first want this, which means something large in exchange and few voters who object. Its constitution may forbid giving up land, as the Honduran Supreme Court said of an earlier special zone plan on grounds of sovereignty. A parliament must vote, and a later government may attack the treaty. Neighbours with interests in the area would then respond. If it all succeeded, the new place would hold land and would need everything else, including a passport other states accept, a country code, a bank that will deal with it and recognition. The founders would remain citizens of their home countries, with those countries' tax and criminal laws still following them, until they gave up that nationality.

It has potential only as a very rare event. The strongest version would be a state already willing to give up a remote, unpopulated and undisputed piece of land, to a body with real backing from other governments, perhaps as part of a settlement of a bigger problem. No such transfer to a new private body has taken place in modern times. If one did, the title would be strong, which explains the high legal and holding figures.

combo-headquarters-immunity.essay:
International organisations have offices in ordinary cities, and the host government agrees not to interfere with them. This is done through a headquarters agreement, a treaty or similar document setting out what the host's police, courts and tax officers may and may not do on those premises. Someone looking for a safe legal position might ask whether a new body could get such a deal, and hold land under it. This combines an extraterritorial spot with an international agreement and the idea of an authority that exists without a territory.

The text of these deals is clear, and the most common belief about them is wrong. People often say that UN headquarters is not on American soil. Section 7 of the 1947 agreement says the district is under the control and authority of the United Nations, and that the federal, state and local law of the United States applies inside it, except as the agreement says otherwise. Section 8 lets the UN make regulations for its work, and an American law that conflicts with them does not apply. Section 9 says the district is inviolable, and American officers may enter to perform official duties only with the consent of the Secretary-General. People who break UN rules may be expelled, and further penalties or arrest depend on American law. The United States also keeps its general control over who enters the country, beyond the transit rights the agreement gives, and in 2025 it refused visas to Palestinian Authority officials. Iran and Russia have argued that this control lets Washington influence the General Assembly's work.

The International Committee of the Red Cross is the most relevant example because it is not an organisation of states. It is a private association under Swiss law that has an international role under the Geneva Conventions. In its agreement with Switzerland of 19 March 1993, the Swiss Federal Council recognises its international juridical personality. Its premises cannot be entered without its consent, it has immunity from legal process and from enforcement with some listed exceptions, and it is exempt from most taxes. Switzerland passed a general law, the Host State Act of 2007, under which it can grant such privileges case by case. Those named as beneficiaries include the World Economic Forum, GAVI and the Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue. CERN, the European physics laboratory founded by a convention of 12 states in 1953 to 1954, shows what such a body can do with land. Its main site at Meyrin was extended across the French border from 1965, so one organisation's campus lies in two countries.

These immunities can be narrowed. In Jam v. International Finance Corporation in 2019, the United States Supreme Court held that international organisations have the same immunity that foreign governments have today, which leaves room for suits over commercial activity. It also noted that an organisation's charter can provide something different, because the statute supplies default rules. Farmers and fishermen in India, who had sued a World Bank lender over a power plant, therefore won on that question, and the Court left open whether their suit could go on under the commercial activity rule. Later courts decided that against them. In 2020 the trial court dismissed the case, because the injury came from the company that built the plant and not from the lender's own commercial activity. The appeals court agreed in 2021, and the Supreme Court declined to hear the case again in 2022.

What is open is whether a new, non-state group could get this treatment. The Swiss law and the Red Cross example show it can be done for a body doing work a government values. Nothing says a host must do so, and no such agreement is known to cover a body whose purpose is to govern residents. Reading these texts, it seems the immunities are functional, meaning they exist so that an organisation can do a particular job, and that they do not make the land into a separate country. A UN premises is inviolable and the land still belongs within New York's legal system. Whether such a grant could expand to a community with homes, families and births is untested.

Follow the path. A founder would first need a mission that a host wants, such as humanitarian, scientific or standards work, and a track record. Then a foreign ministry would negotiate with it. The deal would likely cover offices and staff, and each exception, such as traffic fines and social insurance at the Red Cross, shows the host keeping small powers. Staff keep their nationality and, unless a deal covers it, their taxes at home. A host can also say it bears no responsibility for the body's acts, as Article 20 of the Red Cross agreement does. Above all, the host can withdraw or decline to renew. The people who work there can still be charged for crimes when the head of the organisation waives immunity, as Kofi Annan did in August 2005 for Benon Sevan and Alexander Yakovlev in the Oil-for-Food case.

As a model this has real worth, but it is a model of protected premises. Its strongest version is a respected private body with a useful job, holding a modest campus under a host's law with inviolable buildings. That could be long-lasting and stable. A community that wanted its own courts and citizenship would be asking for something none of these agreements has ever provided.

combo-religious-status.essay:
Religious bodies have held land under special rules for centuries, and governments often treat them with care. This route asks whether a religious identity can add to a territorial claim, through a state's respect for a church, through a tax exemption, or through a religious community running its own town. It combines a host's carve-out, a takeover of local government, and a long-standing authority that does not rest on territory.

Three famous cases are often quoted, and each differs from what a new founder would have. Vatican City became a state in 1929, when Italy recognised the Holy See's sovereignty over 44 hectares in the Lateran Treaty, after a dispute lasting about 60 years. The Holy See had been a ruler and a diplomatic presence for centuries, and it has no modern imitator. Mount Athos in Greece has monks who govern a 335-square-kilometre peninsula, with a monastic history dating back to at least the 9th century, under Greek law and with a church link to the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople. It stays part of Greece. The Order of Malta has diplomatic relations with more than 110 countries, and it signed a treaty with Malta in 1998 for part of Fort St Angelo. Its origins go back to about 1099. Age and the consent of states are what these three share.

The law in the United States is clear in one direction. The Constitution bars government from establishing a religion, and the Supreme Court has applied that to local power. In Larkin v. Grendel's Den in 1982 it struck down a Massachusetts law letting churches veto liquor licences nearby. In Board of Education of Kiryas Joel v. Grumet in 1994 it struck down a New York statute that created a special school district following the lines of a village of Satmar Hasidim. Four justices wrote that this delegated state power to a group defined by common religion, and the Court's majority held that the law went beyond accommodating religion. A state may not hand civic authority to a group chosen by a religious test.

Here comes the point that is more open. Kiryas Joel's village itself was formed under New York's general village law, with boundaries drawn to take in only Satmars, and the Court's decision was aimed at the special school statute. Rajneeshpuram went further. The followers of Bhagwan Rajneesh bought 64,281 acres in Oregon in 1981 for $5.75 million and voted a city into being in May 1982. Oregon's attorney general argued that a city whose land and government lay with one religious group merged church and state. A federal judge ruled against the city in 1985, too late to matter, because criminal cases had ended the commune. Oregon courts later ruled in the city's favour on a separate challenge over land-use rules, and when that litigation closed in 1987 the city was empty, bankrupt and legal under Oregon law. So a religious community can use general laws to form a town, and a court may then ask how far government and religion have fused. Courts decide that by the facts, and the line is not exact.

Colorado City in Arizona, with Hildale over the Utah border, shows the facts of a fusion over decades. A real estate trust of the Fundamentalist Latter-day Saints owned most of the land, and the town was incorporated in 1985. Arizona and Utah began dismantling the church's ownership in 2007. In 2012 the Justice Department sued, saying the town government and police were taking orders from the church. In 2014 a jury found the towns had discriminated against a family that were not members and awarded $5.2 million. The population fell from 4,821 in 2010 to 2,478 in 2020.

Follow how it plays out for a new religious founder. Registering as a church may bring tax exemption, depending on the country, and it does not bring territory. The community buys land and is subject to zoning and building law. If it forms a municipality, its officers must serve everyone, and non-members who move in have rights, as the jury's award to a non-member family in Colorado City showed. Children raise special concerns for child welfare authorities, who keep their full power within religious communities. Citizenship, passports and taxes on members stay with their home countries.

Reading the record, it seems that religious status can win patience from a government and that it cannot substitute for the government's consent. That patience can be real. Greek law's treatment of Athos and Italy's treaty with the Holy See show what a very old religious institution can keep. Outside the United States, a state with an official religion could in principle grant a religious body far more than American law would allow, and this has not been tried for a new group in modern times.

The strongest version is a community that keeps its religious life private, forms no government, and owns land as a charity or company under ordinary law. It can then build a very separate way of life and may last for generations. Mount Athos has lasted far longer, but it governs itself under Greek law, and a new group would not get that by owning land. Recognition as a state is possible for the Holy See only because of a history no new group has.
